'''Laurinda A. Jaffe''' (born January 9, 1952) is an American biologist who is a professor and chair at the [[University of Connecticut]]. Her research considers the physiological mechanisms that regulate [[oocyte]] cell and fertilization. She was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in 2021.

== Early life and education ==
Jaffe was born in [[Pasadena, California]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|last=Uliasz|first=Tracy|date=2019-12-09|title=Curriculum Vitae, Laurinda A. Jaffe {{!}} Department of Cell Biology|url=https://health.uconn.edu/cell-biology/curriculum-vitae-laurinda-a-jaffe/|access-date=2021-05-01|language=en-US}}</ref> Her father, Lionel F. Jaffe, was a senior scientist at the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]] in the [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]]. Her mother, Miriam (Walther) Jaffe, was a professor of astronomy at [[Purdue University]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lionel F. Jaffe|url=https://www.mbl.edu/obituaries/lionel-f-jaffe/|access-date=2021-05-01|website=www.mbl.edu|archive-date=2021-07-27|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210727040945/https://www.mbl.edu/obituaries/lionel-f-jaffe/|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>Lionel F. Jaffe's father was [[Bernard Jaffe]]. {{cite news|newspaper=The New York Times|date=November 22, 1986|page=37, Section 1|title=Obituary. Bernard Jaffe|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1986/11/22/obituaries/bernard-jaffe.html}}</ref> Jaffe was an undergraduate student at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]]. After two years, she moved to Purdue University, where she majored in biology. She was a graduate researcher at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]], where she worked under the supervision of [[Susumu Hagiwara]]. Her doctoral research considered [[polyspermy]] in sea urchin eggs.<ref>{{Cite thesis|title=The fast block to polyspermy in sea urchin egg is electrically mediated|date=1977|language=English|first=Laurinda Ann|last=Jaffe|oclc=1030586902 }}</ref> After graduating, Jaffe worked as a postdoctoral researcher at [[Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution]] with [[Lewis Tilney]] and at the [[University of California, San Diego]] with Meredith Gould.<ref name=":0" />

== Research and career ==
Jaffe studies the physiological mechanisms that regulate [[oocyte]] cell and fertilisation.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Encarnacion|first=Tina|date=2017-07-12|title=Laurinda Jaffe {{!}} Department of Cell Biology|url=https://health.uconn.edu/cell-biology/faculty-and-staff/laurinda-jaffe/|access-date=2021-05-01|language=en-US}}</ref> In particular, she is interested in the [[meiosis]] process that takes place in mammalian ovarian follicles. Meiosis is a type of cell division that prepares the oocyte for fertilisation. The process begins during embryonic development, and then arrests for a prolonged period of time in a prophase. The follicle (including the oocyte and [[granulosa cell]]s) regulates meiotic progression in the oocyte. She identified the proteins ([[Heterotrimeric G protein|G<sub>s</sub> protein]]) and receptors ([[GPR3]]) that are responsible for meiotic prophase arrests. The activity of these proteins result in the production of [[cyclic adenosine monophosphate]] (cAMP), which keeps the cell cycles arrested.<ref name=":1" /> Meanwhile, the granulosa cells within the follicle regulate the hydrolysis of cAMP, a process which involves [[cyclic guanosine monophosphate]] (cGMP) as a [[phosphodiesterase inhibitor]] that maintains high cAMP and meiotic arrest. The signalling system within the [[Granulosa cell tumour|granulosa cell]] switches in response to the [[luteinizing hormone]], which Jaffe has shown lowers the cGMP. This decrease in cGMP can be monitored using [[confocal microscopy]] of mice follicles that express the [[Fluorescence Resonance Energy Transfer]] (FRET) sensor cGi500.<ref name=":1" />

Jaffe has studied the processes that give rise to the [[fibroblast growth factor]] (FGF)-induced inhibition of bone growth. Hormonal signalling decreases the amount of cGMP by inactivating [[NPR2]]. In the ovaries, this causes the cGMP to resume meiotic function, whilst it diminishes growth within bones.<ref name=":1" />
